candidates.attacker_control: Attacker-influenced input is the JDBC URL / resource name: `jdbc:sqlite::resource:<value>` where `<value>` is taken verbatim from the connection URL (or from an application-level "database URL" configuration) and, on class-loader miss, is parsed by `new URL(...)`. An attacker who can influence that value can choose any scheme/host (e.g. `http://`, `https://`, `jar:`, `file:`) and can compute the destination cache path because it is a pure function of `URL.hashCode()` plus `java.io.tmpdir`. Independently, a local user/process able to write to the shared temp directory only needs to pre-create that predictable file (optionally with a recent mtime) to have it opened as the application's database.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The `:resource:` feature is documented for read-only classpath/remote DB access (USAGE.md:57-79), so the URL fetch is intended functionality; exploitability therefore requires an application that lets an attacker influence the resource part of the URL. The `file:` protocol branch (lines 298-304) does not copy the resource, so the temp-file and SSRF aspects do not apply there. `Files.copy(..., REPLACE_EXISTING)` is used rather than an unbounded write, so an arbitrary-file-write impact via a pre-existing symlink was NOT confirmed from source and is not claimed. No runtime testing was performed; the claim that a server without a Last-Modified header yields 0 (thus preferring any pre-existing file) is based on documented java.net.URLConnection semantics and the literal comparison at line 313, not on an observed run.
candidates.impact: Integrity/confidentiality of the data layer, plus a network-access primitive: (a) SSRF/URL-fetch driven by the connection string — the JVM performs requests (or reads arbitrary `file:`/`jar:` URLs) chosen by whoever controls the URL, reaching internal hosts/ports from the server context; (b) the fetched byte stream is handed to SQLite as a database, so attacker-chosen content becomes the database the application reads/writes (silent data substitution, forged rows/schema, and writes into other processes' cached copies since the path is reusable and not deleted); (c) local-attacker substitution: a pre-planted file at the predictable `/tmp/sqlite-jdbc-tmp-<hash>.db` path is preferred by the timestamp logic, so the application opens the attacker's database instead of the intended resource; (d) the cached copy is never removed and is created with default permissions, exposing the referenced database content to other local users.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) The application issues a connection to `jdbc:sqlite::resource:<name-or-URL>` where the resource portion is attacker-influenced (user-supplied "db URL", plugin/config injection, multi-tenant "bring your own SQLite file", or a service that maps a user field into the JDBC URL). (2) For the local-substitution variant: shared/world-writable `java.io.tmpdir` (default on many UNIX deployments) and knowledge of the referenced URL (or of the `:resource:` name that failed classpath lookup, which is resolved to a URL first). (3) No additional privileges are required in the driver itself.
candidates.root_cause: `SQLiteConnection.open()` treats everything after the `:resource:` prefix as a resource name, first resolving it through the thread context class loader and, if that fails, passing it directly to `new URL(resourceName)` with no protocol/host allow-list (SQLiteConnection.java:232-245). `extractResource()` then materializes the referenced content: for non-`file:` protocols it builds the destination as `System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir") + String.format("sqlite-jdbc-tmp-%d.db", resourceAddr.hashCode())` (lines 306-308) — a deterministic, guessable path in a commonly world-writable directory, created with default (typically 0644/umask-derived) permissions and never deleted. If that path already exists, the code returns the pre-existing file whenever `resourceAddr.openConnection().getLastModified()` is not strictly greater than the existing file's mtime (lines 310-322); for resources that send no Last-Modified header (and for many `jar:`/classpath URLs) `getLastModified()` is 0/-1, so any pre-planted file wins. Downloaded content is written with `Files.copy(reader, dbFile.toPath(), REPLACE_EXISTING)` without any integrity verification (lines 334-339); the MD5 comparison that would have detected substitution exists only as commented-out code (lines 324-331). The returned path is then handed to the native layer and opened as the database (lines 247-251, 279-286).
candidates.title: Untrusted URL dereference and predictable temp-file caching in `jdbc:sqlite::resource:` connection handling
candidates.trace: 1) `JDBC.createConnection` -> `JDBC4Connection`/`SQLiteConnection` ctor -> `SQLiteConnection.open(url, origFileName, props)` (SQLiteConnection.java:218). 2) `extractPragmasFromFilename` leaves the `:resource:...` payload intact (lines 511-566). 3) Because `fileName.startsWith(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX)` (line 232), the string after `:resource:` is used as `resourceName`; `contextCL.getResource(resourceName)` is tried, and on failure `resourceAddr = new URL(resourceName)` (lines 236-245) — arbitrary protocol accepted. 4) `extractResource(resourceAddr)` (line 248) returns `new File(resourceAddr.toURI())` directly for `file:` (lines 298-304), otherwise computes the predictable temp path (lines 306-308). 5) If that path exists and its mtime is >= the resource's Last-Modified (0/-1 when absent), the pre-existing file is returned unverified (lines 310-322); otherwise the content is copied over it (lines 337-339) with no checksum and the file persists. 6) The returned absolute path is passed to `NativeDB` construction and `db.open(fileName, config.getOpenModeFlags())` (lines 279-286), i.e. it becomes the SQLite database for all subsequent application queries.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation that an application in this repository's deployment context passes an attacker-influenced `:resource:` value, and no confirmation of the actual temp-directory permissions/JVM umask in a target deployment. Whether `Files.copy`/`newOutputStream` refuses to write through a pre-created symlink at the predictable path was reasoned about but not verified, and no arbitrary-file-write claim is made. The classpath-hit branch (line 237) is unaffected; only the URL fallback (line 240) and the cache logic were assessed.
candidates.weakness_type: Use of Predictable Temporary File / Untrusted URL Fetch (CWE-377, CWE-379, CWE-918)

coverage_summary: Coverage is limited to the assigned 77 model-visible files (75 indexed by the P1 relation index; 2 source files absent from the index; 55 Java files parsed, 0 parse errors, 2236 unresolved calls, no control-flow/data-flow/semantic analysis available per `get_relation_scope`). There are no test sources, no native C sources, and no build execution in this run, so JNI/native behavior could not be verified — all conclusions are from Java source text. Files read and assessed in full or in substantive part: SQLiteConnection.java, SQLiteJDBCLoader.java, OSInfo.java, ProcessRunner.java, ResourceFinder.java, QueryUtils.java, StringUtils.java, ExtendedCommand.java, JDBC.java, SQLiteConnectionConfig.java, Collation.java, Function.java (registration part), NativeDB.java, DB.java, CoreStatement.java, CoreResultSet.java, CorePreparedStatement.java, SafeStmtPtr.java, CoreDatabaseMetaData.java (escape/quote region), JDBC3Connection.java, JDBC3Statement.java, JDBC3Savepoint.java, JDBC3PreparedStatement.java (stream/readBytes region), JDBC3ResultSet.java (spot-checked), JDBC4ResultSet.java (partial), SQLiteConfig.java (constructor/apply/Pragma enum/toProperties), SQLiteDataSource.java (partial), javax/*DataSource and SQLitePooledConnection (partial), demo/, README.md/USAGE.md/NEWS.md, pom.xml, Makefile, workflows (skim), resource/native-image metadata. Not fully reviewed: the bulk of JDBC3DatabaseMetaData.java (91 KB; examined via targeted searches for SQL construction, escaping and pragma interpolation), the `org.sqlite.date.*` package (FastDateParser/FastDatePrinter/FastDateFormat/FormatCache, ~120 KB) beyond imports and deserialization hooks, the remaining portions of JDBC3ResultSet/JDBC4ResultSet, JDBC4Statement/JDBC4Connection/JDBC4PreparedStatement, and the tail of SQLitePooledConnection. Index facts are name-based navigation hints only and were not treated as vulnerability evidence.
limitations: No code was executed: build, tests, and scanners were not run, so no finding is runtime-confirmed; all statements are source-derived.

The P1 index provides no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution (2236 unresolved calls, 2 source files missing from the index), so reachability of `:resource:` URLs from callers inside this repository cannot be established — the driver is a library and the reachable path depends on the host application.

Native/JNI code and the prebuilt SQLite binaries are not present in the snapshot, so behavior at the Java/native boundary (e.g. `sqlite3_open_v2` handling of URI filenames, blob/byte handling) could not be inspected.
No test suite is included, so intended behavior for `:resource:` (documented as read-only classpath/remote DB access in USAGE.md) could not be cross-checked against tests.

The exact semantics of `Files.copy(InputStream, Path, REPLACE_EXISTING)` on a pre-existing symlink and the real-world value of `URLConnection.getLastModified()` for the specific resource types used by a deployment were reasoned from API documentation, not observed.
Directory/server configuration (permissions of `java.io.tmpdir`, whether the deployment is multi-user) is environment-dependent and was not verifiable from the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL injection via unescaped PRAGMA values in `SQLiteConfig.apply()` (`stat.execute(String.format("pragma %s=%s", key, value))`, SQLiteConfig.java:211-221; also the `password`/`hexkey_mode` pragma at 194-208). Pragma names are restricted to the `Pragma` enum, and values arrive from connection Properties/URL parameters.
rejected_leads.reason: The value source is the connecting application (not a remote attacker in the driver's trust boundary), and the executing path (`JDBC3Statement.execute` -> `DB.prepare` -> `sqlite3_prepare_v2`) compiles only the first statement, so an appended `;...` payload in the value is discarded rather than executed. No evidence of an exploitable multi-statement path; not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: Native-library bootstrap: extraction into the temp directory with `deleteOnExit` and deletion of stale `sqlite-<version>*` files (`SQLiteJDBCLoader.cleanup()` / `extractAndLoadLibraryFile`, SQLiteJDBCLoader.java:80-106, 193-242).
rejected_leads.reason: The extracted library name includes a random `UUID`, the file is written via `Files.copy` and then byte-compared with the jar resource (`contentsEquals`, lines 165-183, 227-236), and the version string is sanitized (`replaceAll("[^0-9\\.]", "")`). No attack path with source evidence; the DB-caching path in SQLiteConnection lacks the equivalent verification, which is why that candidate was selected instead.

rejected_leads.lead: Shell command construction in `OSInfo.resolveArmArchType()` (`"find '" + javaHome + "' -name ..."` executed via `/bin/sh -c`, OSInfo.java:207-217) and `ProcessRunner.runAndWaitFor(String)` using `Runtime.exec` with a single string.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only on Linux/ARM when `uname -m` yields no armvX match, and the interpolated value is the JVM's own `java.home` system property (plus `uname -m`/`uname -o` output). No remote attacker input crosses this boundary without the attacker already having code execution; not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL fragments built by string concatenation in the metadata layer, including `quote()` which does not escape single quotes (CoreDatabaseMetaData.java:158-164) and unescaped table-name interpolation in `getColumns` (JDBC3DatabaseMetaData.java:1091) and multiple `PRAGMA ...('...')` statements using `escape()` (e.g. 976, 1423, 1536, 2016).
rejected_leads.reason: Values originate from metadata API arguments or from the same database being inspected; any injection remains inside that database and requires the caller to already supply the hostile identifier. `escape()` does handle single quotes where applied. No cross-boundary impact established.

rejected_leads.lead: `QueryUtils.valuesQuery()` interpolates strings into SQL without escaping (QueryUtils.java:14-40).
rejected_leads.reason: Only caller is `JDBC3DatabaseMetaData.getTypeInfo()` with hard-coded constant lists (JDBC3DatabaseMetaData.java:1767-1771); no attacker-controlled value reaches it.

rejected_leads.lead: Savepoint name interpolation in `JDBC3Connection.setSavepoint(String)`/`releaseSavepoint`/`rollback(Savepoint)` (`SAVEPOINT %s`, `RELEASE SAVEPOINT %s`, `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT %s`, JDBC3Connection.java:244-282) and `JDBC3Savepoint.getSavepointName()` returning the caller's raw name.
rejected_leads.reason: Name is supplied by the calling application (not an external attacker), and `DB.exec` also goes through single-statement `prepare`, so appended statements are not executed. Not submitted.

The only call sites are commented-out verification code (SQLiteConnection.java:324-331); the function is not used for any integrity/authentication decision in the shipped paths, so it is a hardening observation, not a vulnerability.

summary: Repository is the xerial sqlite-jdbc driver at version 3.41.2.1 (pom.xml:7). Reviewed the JDBC connection/URL handling, native-library bootstrap, configuration/pragma handling, statement/result-set layer, metadata layer (via targeted search), pooled-connection wrappers and utility classes. The single strongest evidence-backed issue is the `jdbc:sqlite::resource:` code path in `SQLiteConnection`: an attacker-influenced resource name is dereferenced as an arbitrary URL (no protocol allow-list) and its content is cached in a shared, world-writable temp directory under a fully predictable name derived only from `URL.hashCode()`; an already-existing file at that path is trusted and returned as the database based on a timestamp comparison, with no integrity verification (the MD5 comparison is commented out). This yields an untrusted remote-fetch primitive (SSRF / attacker-chosen content parsed as a database), a local substitution vector for the database actually opened by the application, and a persistent world-readable copy of the resource DB. No runtime confirmation was performed; the finding is a source-evidence lead whose exploitability depends on the application passing an attacker-influenced JDBC URL/resource name.
